---
title: "Clinical Risk Modeling & Survival Analysis"
subtitle: "Three problems from an observational drug-safety analysis, worked on synthetic data"
---

## What this is

An observational comparison of two drug classes on time-to-event outcomes, rebuilt
end to end on synthetic data. It is organised around the three problems that took the
most work to get right, rather than around a list of methods that were applied.

Every number here comes from simulated data. No real patient data, no real results,
no real cohort characteristics appear anywhere in this repository. What is preserved
from the original analysis is the *structure* of the problem: a confounded exposure,
correlated comorbidities, a lab value sitting on the causal pathway, competing events,
month-precision death dates, and two data defects that the cleaning step has to catch.

Because the data is simulated, the true parameter values are known. Every estimate in
these notebooks is checked against the truth it is trying to recover — which is
something the original analysis could never do, and which is the main reason this
version is worth reading.

## The three problems

### 1. Matching ran, but it did not balance

The first propensity score match produced matched pairs and a plausible-looking table,
and several covariates were still imbalanced beyond the conventional threshold. The fix
was tuning the caliper; the lesson was that matching producing output is not the same
as matching producing balance, and that post-match balance has to be verified every
time.

→ [Balance and propensity score matching](notebooks/01-balance-and-psm.qmd)

### 2. Two random forests, two different questions

A random forest on the unmatched cohort with treatment excluded, and one on the matched
cohort with treatment included, give different variable rankings. They are not in
conflict — they answer different questions, and neither one estimates a treatment
effect. Feature importance carries no direction and no significance.

→ [Random forest importance](notebooks/03-random-forest.qmd)

### 3. A competing event that cannot be ignored

Death competes with the outcome of interest: a subject who dies can never go on to
have the event. Censoring those subjects overstates the outcome's cumulative incidence.
This part uses overlap weighting for confounding control and a weighted Fine-Gray model
for the subdistribution hazard, reports the cause-specific hazard alongside it, and
surrounds the primary estimate with the sensitivity analyses that have to agree with it
before it means anything.

→ [Competing risks](notebooks/05-competing-risks.qmd)

## The two studies

The work divides into two designs that handle confounding differently.

| | Study A | Study B |
|---|---|---|
| Confounding control | 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching on the propensity score | Overlap weighting |
| Outcome models | Nested Cox proportional hazards ladder | Fine-Gray and cause-specific Cox |
| Competing risks | Not modelled | Death as a competing event |
| Machine learning | Random forest feature importance | — |

Study B is where the design moved after Study A: matching had to chase balance by
tightening a caliper, and paid for it in discarded subjects. Overlap weighting achieves
balance by construction and keeps everybody.

3. [Cox models](notebooks/02-cox-models.qmd) — Study A outcome models

## Reproducing it

```bash
Rscript -e 'renv::restore()'
quarto render
```

The synthetic cohorts are generated from a fixed seed on first use and cached to
`data/synthetic/`. That directory is not tracked: it is derived, it rebuilds in about
two seconds, and a repository that ships a data file it cannot regenerate is one you
cannot check.
